'''Zygmunt Steuermann''' (5 February 1899 – December 1941) was a Polish [[association football|footballer]] who played as a [[forward (association football)|forward]].<ref>{{NFT|47455|access-date=17 February 2021}}</ref> He was one of the most renowned members of the [[Hasmonea Lwów]] football club.

==Life==
{{More citations needed|sectioned|date=July 2023}}
Born in [[Sambir|Sambor]], then in Austro-Hungarian [[Galicia (Central Europe)|Galicia]], Steuermann was Jewish<ref name="auto">{{Cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/blog/2019/may/06/remembering-the-cream-of-jewish-footballing-talent-killed-in-the-holocaust|title=Remembering the cream of Jewish footballing talent killed in the Holocaust|first=David|last=Bolchover|newspaper=The Guardian |date=6 May 2019|via=www.theguardian.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/ahead-of-match-with-israel-poland-honors-murdered-jewish-sport-legend-591924|title=Ahead of match with Israel, Poland honors murdered Jewish sport legend|website=JPost.com|date=10 June 2019 |accessdate=8 July 2023}}</ref> and a member of a Polonized Jewish family. His older brother was pianist [[Eduard Steuermann]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Melnyk |first1=Lidia |chapter = Steuermann, Gimpel, Baller – Between the Vienna Dream and Hollywood Reality: World-Famous Jewish Pianists and Their Routes From Galicia to Vienna and the USA |editor-last= Pijarowska | editor-first = Aleksandra |title=Music – The Cultural Bridge: Essence, Context, References |date=2021 |publisher=[[Karol Lipiński Academy of Music]] |location=[[Wrocław]] |page=113 |url=https://dbc.wroc.pl/Content/110174/music_the_cultural_bridge.pdf#page=114 |access-date=30 June 2022}}</ref> His older sister was the actress and screenwriter [[Salka Viertel]]. As a child, he was nicknamed Dusko.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Rifkind |first1=Donna |title=The Sun and Her Stars: Salka Viertel and Hitler's Exiles in the Golden Age of Hollywood |date=28 January 2020 |publisher=[[Other Press]] |location=New York |isbn=978-1590517215 |oclc = 1099570013 | page=171 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f33HDwAAQBAJ&q=zygmunt%20nickname%20 |access-date=26 June 2022}}</ref>

At the age of 12, he joined the local Korona Sambor. During [[World War I]], he fled to [[Vienna]], where he continued his training in a variety of sport clubs, including Gersthof Wien, Germania Wien, and Amateure Wien. After the war, he returned to Poland and in 1920 started a semi-professional career in Korona Sambor.<ref>{{cite web |title=STEUERMANN Zygmunt |url=https://polska-pilka.pl/reprezentanci/s/steuermann-zygmunt?highlight=WyJzdGV1ZXJtYW5uIl0= |website=polska-pilka.pl |access-date=27 November 2024 |language=pl}}</ref> During the following year, he moved to [[Lwów]] (modern Lviv, [[Ukraine]]), where he joined the [[ŻKS Lwów]] sports club. In 1923, he was transferred to [[Hasmonea Lwów]], the most important Jewish football club in Poland and one of the four Lwów-based clubs playing in the first league.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.ynetnews.com/articles/0,7340,L-3931288,00.html|title=Anti-Semitism feared ahead of Euro 2012|date=8 August 2010|website=Ynetnews |last1=Beck |first1=Eldad }}</ref> He remained one of the most notable players of that club until 1932, when he joined [[Legia Warsaw]].

He also played twice in the [[Poland national football team|Poland national team]], scoring four goals: [[Hat-trick|three in a match]] against Turkey in 1926<ref name="auto"/> and one against the USA in 1928.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=f33HDwAAQBAJ&q=Zygmunt+Steuermann+jewish&pg=PA157|title=The Sun and Her Stars: Salka Viertel and Hitler's Exiles in the Golden Age of Hollywood|first=Donna|last=Rifkind|date=8 September 2020|publisher=Other Press, LLC|isbn=9781590517215|via=Google Books}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=3O80DwAAQBAJ&q=Zygmunt+Steuermann+jewish&pg=PT94|title=Identity, Attachment and Resilience: Exploring Three Generations of a Polish Family|first=Antonia|last=Bifulco|date=6 September 2017|publisher=Routledge|isbn=9781351789509|via=Google Books}}</ref> He was one of only two first-timers in the history of the Poland national team to score a [[hat-trick]] in the first match, the other being [[Józef Korbas]] (in 1937 against Bulgaria).

During the [[Invasion of Poland (1939)|Nazi and Soviet invasion of Poland in 1939]], he fled Warsaw and settled in his hometown, which was then annexed by the [[USSR]]. He returned to Korona Sambor, which was soon afterwards closed down and recreated as [[Dinamo Sambor]] by the Soviet authorities. Following the [[Nazi]] take-over of [[eastern Poland]], he was arrested and sent to the [[Lemberg Ghetto]], where he died in December 1941 aged 42.
